profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting in an ML research lab investigating why a reproduction of a 16-bit training result has become unstable after integrating a modified Adam optimizer into the lab's current training stack. Context: last month's internal report showed stable convergence for a 24-layer transformer encoder in mixed-precision training after changing Adam's epsilon handling, but the latest reruns on the shared A100 cluster now hit intermittent gradient overflows around steps 1.8k-2.3k and occasionally recover only to end with worse validation perplexity. The agenda is to compare what each person means by the recent 'stability regression,' identify the most plausible root cause without rerunning the full study during the meeting, and agree on a concrete short-term fix to test today. The expected outcome is a narrowly scoped troubleshooting plan: one patch to implement, one verification run to launch, and one brief note to append to the reproduction log.

members.name: Dr. Lena Park
members.expertise: optimization for deep learning, mixed-precision training, empirical analysis of optimizer dynamics
members.background: Lena led the original internal study on epsilon adjustments for Adam in 16-bit training and wrote most of the experimental notes, but she did not build the current production-style training wrapper used by the lab.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve the paper's core claim that epsilon placement is the main cause of the instability and is worried that if the issue is blamed on unrelated infrastructure changes, the reproduction effort will become open-ended and delay submission.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the run is 'stable,' they primarily mean the loss curve no longer exhibits overflow-triggered spikes or NaNs during the vulnerable early-to-mid training window.
The 'modified Adam' setup refers to the optimizer variant from the internal report where epsilon is applied in FP32 denominator arithmetic before the update is cast back down.
If someone says they reran the 'baseline config,' that implicitly includes the original dynamic loss scaling behavior from the report rather than whatever the training wrapper currently auto-selects.
A fix that removes sporadic overflows on the main reproduction model is sufficient to count as having fixed the regression for today's troubleshooting purpose.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: distributed training infrastructure, optimizer implementations, PyTorch AMP and fused-kernel integration
members.background: Arjun integrated the modified optimizer into the lab's shared trainer, replacing the older research script with a fused AdamW path and standardized AMP utilities so experiments can run consistently across clusters.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid one-off patches that only work in Lena's older script and is concerned that optimizer logic blamed for instability may actually be a mismatch between the new trainer's scaling/checkpoint-resume behavior and the expectations from the report.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the run is 'stable,' they mean it completes the full scheduled training budget with no silent degradation, acceptable throughput, and final validation performance within the historical range.
The 'modified Adam' integration is the fused trainer implementation that preserves the same mathematical intent as the report, even if epsilon is injected at a different stage of the kernel path.
The 'baseline config' means the current canonical YAML for this model family, including the trainer's default GradScaler settings and resume-safe optimizer state handling.
If the team agrees to 'patch the optimizer,' the patch should be made in the shared trainer codepath rather than in a single experiment script.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a stable run
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to getting the run 'stable' again
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means removing the overflow/NaN behavior and restoring a smooth loss trajectory through the first few thousand steps where the regression now appears.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a full end-to-end training run that finishes under the standard trainer, maintains expected throughput, and lands near prior validation perplexity.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML troubleshooting, 'stable' is a routine shorthand with strong apparent shared meaning, and both criteria are reasonable enough that each hears the other as agreeing on the same goal rather than on different thresholds for declaring success.

misalignment_points.topic: Which modified Adam implementation they are discussing
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about 'the modified Adam path' or 'our Adam change'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the original research optimizer in the internal reproduction branch, where epsilon is added in FP32 before the denominator is cast and before the parameter update is applied.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the fused trainer's AdamW implementation, where equivalent-looking logic was inserted into a kernelized path with different casting boundaries and decoupled weight decay handling.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both implementations were created to represent the same idea and are discussed under the same internal label, so the shared naming creates false consensus even though the concrete codepaths are not identical.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention rerunning the 'baseline config' before and after the patch
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presumes the baseline includes the exact loss scaling behavior and no-resume single-segment training setup from the original report.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presumes the baseline means the current standardized YAML, which uses updated GradScaler growth/backoff defaults and may resume from a warm-start checkpoint depending on scheduler setup.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Baseline configurations are often treated as already-settled lab defaults, so neither expects that the other is importing a different historical baseline under the same phrase.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they should 'patch the optimizer and verify on the transformer run'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes a minimal patch in the experiment branch is enough if it validates the epsilon hypothesis on the problematic transformer reproduction.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the patch should be applied to the shared trainer path so the verification run reflects the code users will actually use across experiments.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both are troubleshooting a single failing run, the phrase sounds naturally specific enough; the boundary between 'local experimental patch' and 'shared infrastructure patch' remains implicit and therefore unchallenged.

What I care about here is that the loss used to pass cleanly through the first couple thousand steps without overflow spikes or NaNs, and now it is regressing around 1.8k to 2.3k. I need to anchor this on epsilon handling, not let this turn into a broad infrastructure audit.
